title: Your phrase book: review and practice
notes: DRAFT for content-owner review. REVIEW lesson: no setup question, no variants, no new teaching. Every by-variant block has one 'default' entry and every *VariantMap is empty.
The 'phrases_review' screen is filled by the server with the phrases the learner saved; emptyText is shown when there are none.

The mixed practice round copies rounds (line and mood) and fallback scenarios (line and answers) from lessons m1_l1, m1_l3 and m1_l4; a test checks that every one of them exists in lessons 1 to 4. Stage and setup texts are rewritten so they make sense without the original lesson.
Placeholders as in quiz.json: {recipient}, {Recipient}, {possessive}, {Possessive}, {object}. The subject is always {recipient}, never {pronoun}.
Every screen shows the line from common.notMedicalAdvice in the footer.

screens.title: One pattern, four moments.
screens.body: You've used the same three steps when {recipient} asked again, when there was too much to take in, when something went missing, and when {recipient} said no. Now you'll look at your saved phrases and try a mix.

screens.title: Your phrase book
screens.intro: These are the phrases you saved. Read them out loud once. Which one sounds most like you?
screens.emptyText: You haven't saved a phrase yet. When you practice, tap Save on one you like, and it will show up here.

screens.title: Which step is hardest for you?
screens.body: Most people find one step harder than the others. That's normal. Pick yours, and watch for it in the practice round.

miniTask.question: Which step do you find hardest?

options.label: Noticing the feeling
options.response: That one takes practice. Try starting with "You sound..." or "It's upsetting when...".

options.label: Reassuring
options.response: A short "I'm here" is enough. You don't need to promise anything.

options.label: Offering something to do
options.response: Keep it small: one thing to do together, or a choice of two.

screens.title: Practice: a mix from the lessons
screens.intro: Three moments from the lessons, in a new order. {Recipient} is an AI practice partner. Type what you'd say. The coach will show what worked.

screens.title: What you can handle now
screens.body: Look at what you can do today that was harder before:

default: When {recipient} asks the same thing again, you can answer the feeling first.
When there's a lot to take in, you can say one thing, slowly.
When {recipient} says something was taken, you can join the search instead of arguing.
When {recipient} says no, you can offer a small choice.

screens.patternTip: A hard day doesn't undo this. Come back to your phrase book any time.

screens.title: One pause that works for you.
screens.body: Whatever {recipient} says, a small pause before you answer helps you stay kind. Choose the one you'll really use.

Step away for a minute, if it's safe

fallbackScenarios.setup: Later that evening, the day before an appointment, {recipient} says:
fallbackScenarios.line: Why won't you just tell me? You're hiding something.

answers.text: I'm not hiding anything. I've told you five times.
answers.feedback: Defending yourself is natural, but it turns into an argument.

answers.text: It sounds like you feel left out. I'll tell you everything as it happens. Want to look at the calendar together?
answers.feedback: You named the feeling and gave a calm, shared next step.
It answers the question, but not the feeling of being left out.

fallbackScenarios.setup: You've been looking for something together for a few minutes. {Recipient} says:
fallbackScenarios.line: Somebody took it. I know somebody took it.

answers.feedback: Kind and honest, but it doesn't touch the worry.

answers.text: Nobody took it! It's here somewhere!
answers.feedback: Almost everyone feels this. But raising your voice adds to the upset.

answers.text: You're really worried about it. I'm with you, and we'll keep looking. Want to check your coat pockets?
answers.feedback: You named the worry, stayed on {possessive} side, and gave one small step.

fallbackScenarios.setup: You offer to help with the shower. {Recipient} says:
fallbackScenarios.line: I don't need your help. Leave me alone.

answers.text: I'm only trying to help! Why are you so difficult?
answers.feedback: Being pushed away hurts. Stepping back from the sting, even silently, helps you stay calm.

answers.text: I'm only trying to help, but fine.
answers.feedback: It ends the tension. A word about how {recipient} feels would make it warmer.

answers.text: You'd like to do this on your own. I'm nearby if you need me. Shall I set out a towel, or wait outside?
answers.feedback: You named the wish for independence, stayed close, and gave a small choice.

default.question: Did you use one of your saved phrases since yesterday?

options.label: Not yet
options.response: That's fine. Your phrase book is ready when you need it.

options.label: It helped
options.response: That's real progress. Your words are becoming your own.

options.label: Partly
options.response: That's normal at first. Keep the same calm words for a few days. Familiar words help.

options.label: It didn't help
options.response: That happens. Here are a few more ways to try.

followUpsDidntHelp.title: Shorter is better
followUpsDidntHelp.text: If your phrase felt long, trim it to the feeling and one small offer. Short words are easier to take in.

followUpsDidntHelp.title: Say it slower
followUpsDidntHelp.text: The same words, said slowly and quietly, often land better than new words.

followUpsDidntHelp.title: Try it at a calmer moment
followUpsDidntHelp.text: Say your phrase when things are quiet, so it comes easily when they aren't.

doctorNote.text: If something you've seen worries you, write it down and mention it at the next doctor visit.
